chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhl from Ahmad ibn A'idh from Muhammad ibn Hakim who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) and said: 'For the woman who does not menstruate, similar to her and who has not menstruated, what is her waiting period?' He said: 'Three months.' I said: 'But she is uncertain (about the duration).' He said: 'She observes the end of the two periods; she observes nine months.' I said: 'But she is uncertain.' He said: 'There is no uncertainty upon her, because Allah, Exalted and Glorious, has set a time for pregnancy, so there is no uncertainty after it.'
And whoever wishes to divorce the woman of uncertain status, he should wait for her for three months, then divorce her if he wishes. That which indicates this is what he narrated.

key_terms.الْأَجَلَيْنِ: The two periods (referring to the minimum and maximum durations)
key_terms.الْمَرْأَةُ الَّتِي لَا تَحِيضُ: The woman who does not menstruate
key_terms.الْمُسْتَرَابَةِ: The woman of uncertain status (regarding pregnancy/duration)

ai.seo_question: What is the Iddah period for a woman who does not menstruate according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Rida (or al-Jawad, depending on the specific chain context often associated with this ruling) clarifies the 'Iddah for a woman who does not menstruate, establishing three months as the baseline. The Imam further explains that if pregnancy is suspected, the period extends to nine months, citing the divine principle that pregnancy has a fixed maximum duration, thereby removing uncertainty once that limit is passed. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential reliance on natural biological limits to resolve legal ambiguities in personal status law.
